Committee for examination and report.

The Press Communiqué appeared in the leading newspapers

            The Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 2001(see Annexure-I) seeks to amend the Companies Act, 1956 by way of inserting an additional Part (Part-IX-A) relating to the formation/registration of Producer Companies and all matters relating thereto.  The Bill, in effect introduces a new

economic enterprise1 known as “Producer Company” in the Companies Act, 1956.
 
1.1       The principal aim of the proposed legislation is to provide for formation and registration of producer companies, whichhas unique blend of many features of a limited company with the principles and practices of mutual assistance and cooperation to operate under a regulatory framework
similar to that of private limited companies.
 
1.2       The Bill will also enable incorporation of cooperative as producer companies and conversion of existing cooperatives into producer companies.
 
2.0
              A producer company can be formed/registered by any of the following entities/manner: -
 
(i)                  any ten or more primary producers;
(ii)                any two producer institutions;
(iii)               a combination of ten or more primary producers and producer institution(s);and
(iv)              conversion of producer cooperative of inter-state nature, if two-thirds of its  members voluntarily resolve to do so.
 
2.1.0    The objects of a producer company inter alia include production, processing, manufacture and sale of primary produce as well as allied matters.  The owners/members of Producer Company have necessarily to be “primary producers”.  In nutshell producer company deal with produce of its
Members.
 
2.1.1    The Primary producers are those individuals who are engaged in an activity connected with or relatable to primary produce [Section 581 A (k)  Clause 2 of the Bill].
 
2.1.2    Primary produce as defined in the Bill [Section 581A(j) Clause2] includes products of agriculture, horticulture, floriculture, pisciculture, viticulture, forestry, forest products, revegetation, bee-raising, farming, plantation products, animal husbandry and related field as well as the products
of cottage industry, artisans, etc.

3.0       The salient features of the proposed legislation are as categorized below: -
 
(i)
                  It enables primary producers to form specially structured Producer Company on the basis of principles of mutual assistance and provides purely a voluntary option for existing cooperatives to become Producer Companies.
(ii)                Ten or more natural persons who are producers, two or more producer institutions or a combination of both can also form Producer Companies;
(iii)               This act gives option to such of those inter-state co-operatives2 desirous of registering as Producer Companies to do so;
(iv)              In case of Company formed of individuals member shall have single vote irrespective of share holding, where the Company is formed exclusively by producer institutions the voting right may be computed on the basis of participation in the business, and incase of Company formed
of individuals and institutions there shall only be a single vote for every member;
(v)                In order to further its objectives the Producer Company may collaborate to form subsidiaries, joint ventures etc.
(vi)              Board of Directors of the Producer Company are elected by the General Body. Provision for co-option of expert Directors has been provided;
(vii)             The Board of Directors shall appoint the Chief Executive of the Producer Company.  Other employees of the company will be appointed by the Chief Executive in accordance with the powers delegated to him by the Board;
(viii)           The Board of Directors shall be responsible and accountable to conduct timely audit, election and general body meetings.
(ix)              Producer Company may provide provisions for “Special Users Right” to its active members in the articles of association;
(x)                Every member of a Producer Company must participate in the Company’s business.  The articles of association may establish minimal levels of the participation and may provide conditions under which those who do not meet those levels, or who cease to participate, may be made
ineligible to hold office, to vote or to continue their membership;
(xi)              Producer Companies will form their own articles of association suiting to their own business and operational needs; and
(xii)             Dispute settlement shall be by simple process of Arbitration and Conciliation.
 
4.0       The Bill is almost akin to the draft legislation formulated by the High Powered Committee for Formation and Conversion of Cooperative Business into Companies on the basis of its observations and recommendations.  The draft legislation was also annexed to its Report.
 
4.1.0    The said High Powered Committee was constituted in the background to the proposed legislation on 1 November 1999, which in turn submitted its Report on 15 March, 2000.
 
4.1.1    The Alagh Committee was of an eight member body headed by Dr. Y.K. Alagh.  The Committee had also appointed a five-member sub-Committee comprising of officers from Departments of Company Affairs, Legal Affairs, Rural Development and Agriculture and Cooperation to
recommend a draft legislation to it.
 
4.2.0    The Alagh Committee had observed that post-independence cooperatives have often become vehicles for Government programmes, operating with substantial government funds and personnel.  Government funding has often led to Government control leading to bureaucratization and
political interference.
 
4.2.1    In the era of liberalisation and globalisation of Indian economy, producer cooperatives are trying for its growth & development in competitive environment.  It is due to the fact that rural producer cooperatives are not equipped with resources, skill, opportunity,  they are not able to
withstand the competition.  Moreover, under the existing cooperative laws even the large producer cooperatives find it extremely difficult to face increasingly stiff competition from their corporate counterparts due to lack of a level playing field. The Committee, therefore, suggested Producer
Company as an alternative for those producer cooperatives, which opt voluntarily to operate effectively in a competitive environment.
 
5.0       In the liberalised economy, the producer cooperatives as an independent business entity are at a disadvantageous position as compared to other economic entities dealing with the same produce such as MNCs.  The factors attributed for the same by the Department of Company Affairs are
limited assets, resources, education access to advance technology and  bureaucratic control, etc. The Department of Company Affairs has stated in their background note that cooperative laws (both State & Central) vests enormous powers with Registrar of Cooperatives, which are often misused
thereby hampering growth and development of the cooperatives. Therefore Government feels the need to provide for option to the cooperatives to operate within the domain of Company Law.
 
5.1       The producer companies have to be registered with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 1956, even if the Producers Co-operatives are  registered bodies,  with Registrar of Cooperative Societies under Societies Registration Act, 1860 before becoming a producer
company.
           
6.0       The cooperative sector in India has emerged as one of the largest 3
 in the world with 5.28 lakh societies of various types with a membership of 22.8767 crore and working capital of Rs.285643.35 crores as on 31 March 2001.  Almost hundred per cent villages and sixty-seven of the rural
household are covered under the cooperative fold.  Their contribution in ushering in green and white Revolutions in the country is well known.
 
6.1       Producer Cooperatives form one-third of total cooperatives in India.  As per the statistics compiled by National Cooperative Union of India (NCUI), the total number of producer cooperatives is 150962 out of total cooperatives i.e. 528228.  [Source: Indian Cooperative Movement- A profile
2001: Indian Cooperative  Movement at a Glance (1999-2000)].
 
6.2       The National Policy on Cooperatives enumerates the development of cooperatives as institutions.  The first attempt to institutionalize cooperatives began in the year 1904.  Under the Government of India Act, 1919 the subject  of cooperation was transferred to the then Provinces, which
were authorised to enact their own cooperative laws.  Currently, “Cooperative Societies” is a State subject under Entry 32 of State List of the Constitution.  Accordingly,  almost all the States have their own laws on Cooperative Societies.
 
6.3       The Multi-Unit Cooperative Societies Act, 1942 was enacted by the Union Government to govern operations of cooperative societies where membership was from more than one province which was subsequently replaced by Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, 1984.  The Multi-State
Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000 to replace the Act of 1984 is pending in the Lok Sabha to amend the Act of 1984.  The Multi-State Cooperative is in Union List  (entry No. 44)

6.4       The Alagh Committee had pointed out that in other parts of the World viz- Denmark, Switzerland, United States of America and Zimbabwe, cooperatives and similar forms of enterprises operate under Corporate Law which allows cooperatives the freedom to compete  with other economic
enterprises.
 
6.5       Some States (i.e. Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Bihar) have attempted to counter the problems inherent in their State laws on Cooperatives by enacting progressive parallel legislations.  Such a route will take too long to ensure that producer cooperatives have a viable
and sustainable place in the economy of the country.
 
6.6       The need for bringing in such legislations at Central level was felt owing to the rationale stated above.
 
7.0       The Committee in its meeting held on February 18, 2002 heard the views of the following representatives of the cooperative movement in the country:
   
               i)   Dr S.S. Sisodia, President, National Co-operative Union of India (NCUI)
              ii)   Dr Amrita Patel, Chairperson, National Dairy Development Board (NDDB)
             iii)   Shri V.N. Rai, Managing Director, Krishak Bharati Co-operative Limited (KRIBCO)
 
7.1       During his deposition, the President of NCUI had raised the following points:
 
(i)
                  The proposed legislation is not in the interest of cooperative movement and is also against its philosophy. It would send a wrong signal to the said movement across the country;
(ii)                Member’s control and participation which is the basic ethos of the cooperative form of organisation is absent in the Companies Act as voting by proxy is available therein. Therefore, it is most likely that the producer companies might be monopolised and hijacked by a few
individuals having large share holdings by misusing the provision of proxy vote available under the Companies Act;
(iii)               There is no provision in the Companies Act that provides for penalising a Producer Company that does not either follow the cooperative principles or flouts any of them;
(iv)              The Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000 does not have a corresponding enabling provision for conversion of cooperative societies into producer companies;
(v)                There is no need of the legislation as under clause 19 of the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000, societies can form their subsidiary institutions which may be registered under any other law including Companies Act; and
(vi)              The Alagh Committee neither held any consultations nor invited comments or responses of NCUI, which is an apex body of the cooperative movement in India on the subject of formation of Producer Companies under the Companies Act.
 
7.2.0    The Chairperson of NDDB was very emphatic in her presentation conveying that the Bill in question is very important for the growth and benefit of the cooperatives in the present liberalized economic scenario. She specifically narrated the experience of NDDB in promoting the dairy
cooperatives, the obstacles faced by them in view of the restrictive cooperative Acts, and the need for providing them a level playing field at a time when they were faced with increasing competition. She was of the view that the existing Cooperative Acts were based on a law formulated to meet
the needs of small village level cooperatives and were ill suited to the current needs of the cooperatives. She mentioned that although some States had taken the initiative to enact parallel cooperative laws meant for self-reliant cooperatives, the reforms in cooperative legislations had been
extremely slow. She also indicated that the proposed producer company legislation was extremely opportune and necessary if the impact of liberalization and globalisation was to be dealt with professionally and if the interests of our rural producers  was  to be protected.
 
7.2.1    She suggested to the Committee to consider bringing about the following two changes in the Bill:
(i)                  Omission of clause 581D(1)(c) which provides for single vote for every member of a Producer Company formed by a combination of producer institutions and individuals and other consequential changes explaining that such a provision is prone to misuse; and
(ii)                Need for suitable change in 581P(1)(6) qualifying the term expert directors to be co-opted on the board of a Producer Companies so as to prevent the misuse of the provision for co-option.
 
7.2.2    To a query by the Chairman of the Committee on whether the proposed Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000 will be able to meet the requirement of the cooperative movement instead of the Producer Companies Bill, she replied that the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000
will have limited utility. She said that it will benefit only those cooperatives which have members in more than one State whereas the Bill now being considered addresses the need of organizations whose objects extend to more than one state and thus will meet a different purpose.
 
7.2.3    Responding to the question whether there was any significant opposition to the Bill from certain quarters, she said that since the NCUI had expressed some concerns with respect to the Bill.  On the advice of the then Agriculture Minister Shri Nitish Kumar, the points raised by NCUI were
discussed with them.
 
7.3       The Managing Director of KRIBCO did not have any specific points to offer except categorically conveying KRIBCO’s support to the Bill.
 
 7.4      The Committee also considered replies/clarifications of the Department of Company Affairs on the apprehensions/comments/suggestions raised by the witnesses in the meeting of the Committee as well as in their subsequent memoranda and on the responses/suggestions received from
various organizations such as Co-operative Development Foundation (CDF), Hyderabad, Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad (IIMA), All India Handloom Fabric Marketing Co-operative Society Limited and National Co-operative Dairy Federation of India (NCDFI) (see Annexure-II).

9.3.7    The Committee pointed out that the above provision restricts the investment of general reserves of the company in approved securities, Government units, bonds etc. and the investment in zero-risk areas may not entail much profit to the members of producer companies whereas wider

9.3.8    In response to the Committee’s suggestion, the Department of Company Affairs has submitted their reply as following
 
The producer companies will be having generally the features of Co-operative Society.  As such the investment of co-operatives should not be made in a risky manner and may be invested as provided in clause 581ZL of the Bill. Similar provisions for investment of funds are there in other
Acts also such as the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912 and the State Agricultural Credit Cooperation Act, 1968 etc. In addition to this we may add in sub-section (1) of Section 581ZL the following words – ‘or as may be prescribed by the Government.’
 
This will enable the Government to prescribe any mode in which the investment can be made by the producer companies in addition to the existing one proposed in the Bill.

    The Section deals with amalgamation, merger or division of producer company.
9.3.11  While discussing the section, the Committee pointed out that the norms in respect of valuation of assets at the time of merger and amalgamation was conspicuously absent in the Bill.  The Committee further wanted to know whether the provision relating to the jurisdictional aspect of High
Court in respect of  the cases relating to Producer Company was incorporated in the Bill.  The Committee directed the Department of Company Affairs to submit a note on those aspects for its consideration.
 
9.3.12  The reply of the Department of Company Affairs to these two queries of the Committee are as below:
 
Section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956, deals with power to compromise and arrangement with creditors and members in case of merger/amalgamation etc., no such valuation clause finds place (sic).  There are no rules for valuation of assets under the Companies Act, 1956.  As such it is
not appropriate to introduce any such new provision for the Producer Companies.  However, the assets of the companies are evaluated according to accounting principles and exchange ratio is arrived at.  This is a matter of mutual agreement between members and creditors.  The details
will be available to all concerned before they exercise their power to vote.  The company will follow the normal procedure for getting the assets evaluated for the purpose of arriving at exchange ratio. No specific clause is necessary.
 
Even in the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Bill, 2000 also no provision for valuation of assets has been provided. It is based on mutual agreement.  However, normal accounting principles and business ethics will have to be kept in view while considering the amalgamation.  In view of

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            During the last decade, changes have taken place in the Indian economy, in the communication and transportation infrastructures, as well as in the method of commerce, banking and international trade.  Liberalization of the economy is in the process of changing the terms of trade between
rural and urban, labour and industry, finance and commerce.  Biotechnology, the information revolution, computerization can all be used to raise the standard of living of the rural asses and ultimately link this economic with regional, national and global demand.  Institutions are needed to link the
rural economy with the emerging new opportunities.  Rural producers are at a potentional disadvantage given their generally limited assets, resources, education and access to advanced technology.  In the present competitive scenario, if cooperative enterprises are to continue to serve rural
producers, they require an alternative to the institutional form presently available under Law.
            2. Keeping all this in view Government constituted a Committee consisting of experts led by Dr. Y.K. Alagh, Economist, former Union Minister to examine and make recommendations with regard to (a) framing a legislation which would enable incorporation of cooperatives as companies
and conversion of existing cooperatives into companies and (b) ensuring that the proposed legislation accommodates the unique elements of cooperative business within a regulatory framework similar to that of companies.  The Committee had a series of meeting during which it interacted with,
and received responses from various cooperatives, institutes and individuals.
 
            3.  On the basis of the recommendations of the Committee the present Bill has been prepared with the main objective of facilitating formation of cooperative business as companies and to convert existing business into companies.  The salient features of the Bill are:
          (i)           to offer a statutory and regulatory framework that creates the potential for producer-owned enterpirses to compete with other enterprises on a competitive footing.  The Companies Act envisages and provides for various forms of Companies including private limited, public limited,
trusteeship companies and nidhis, each with specific and appropriate provisions applicable to them.
 
           (ii)         to provide for the formation and registration of producer companies which include the mutual assistance and co-operative principles within the more liberal regulatory framework afforded by the Company Law with suitable adaptations.
         
           (iii)        to provide an opportunity to cooperative institutions to voluntarily transform themselves into the new form of producer companies.
 
            (iv)       Under the Bill conversion of co-operatives to producer companies is purely voluntary.
 
(v)
                Member equity may not be publicly traded, but may only be transferred, with the approval of the producer company’s Board of Directors.  Producer Companies would not be vulnerable to the takeover by multinationals or other companies.
 
(vi)
              The conversion option by co-operative society to producer company can be exercised only if two-thirds of the Members of the concerned society vote in favour of a resolution to that effect.
 
(vii)             The new form of Company is designated as “producer company” to indicate that only certain categories of persons can participate in the ownership of such Companies.  The members of the Producer Company have necessarily to be “primary producers”’ that is persons engaged in
an activity connected with, or relatable to, primary produce.
 
(viii)           The objects of a producer company have been defined to include, among other things, production, processing, manufacture and sale of primary produce as well as allied matters.
 
4.  The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.
